text: People act like having a startup fail is the worst thing that can happen to you. And man, that's not even in the top 10. It's bad, I've done it, it's awful.
speaker: Eric Ries
context: Lenny asks Eric about his career and current work. Eric reflects on the mental health challenges facing entrepreneurs and different types of business failures. He explains that while startup failure is painful, being trapped in a 'zombie' company that won't die but also won't succeed is far worse for founders' wellbeing. Eric emphasizes the often-overlooked psychological toll of building companies that become forces founders no longer believe in.
text_ko: 사람들이 스타트업(startup)이 실패하면 인생에서 가장 최악의 일인 것처럼 말해요. 근데 솔직히 그건 최악의 10위권에도 못 들어요. 물론 안 좋죠, 저도 겪어봤는데 정말 끔찍했어요.
text_zh: 大家好像觉得创业失败是天塌下来的事儿。哥们儿，这连前十都排不上。确实很糟心，我经历过，真的很难受。
text_es: La gente actúa como si que te fracase una startup fuera lo peor que te puede pasar en la vida. Y oye, eso ni siquiera está en el top 10. Está mal, lo he vivido, es horrible.
key_sentence: having a startup fail is the worst thing that can happen to you.
original_text: People act like having a startup fail is the worst thing that can happen to you. And man, that's not even in the top 10. It's bad, I've done it, it's awful. It's really bad, but far worse is to be in a company that won't die, a zombie, undead company that you hate, but you can't leave. Oof, have I met people like that, and we're having a mental health crisis among founders that's not talked about enough.

text: And I would go and have these meetings, and I'm not making this up, people would yell at me in the meeting. I would get yelled at. In fact, I would be asked not very kindly to leave, and I'd be like, "I don't understand.
speaker: Eric Ries
context: Lenny asks Eric about his early career and how he didn't expect to have such impact on startup culture. Eric describes the early days before Lean Startup became popular, when he would meet with VCs and startup teams to share his engineering methods. His practices of shipping code 50 times per day seemed impossible to most people at the time, leading to hostile reactions in meetings where people literally asked him to leave.
text_ko: 회의에 가서 이런 미팅들을 했는데, 이건 꾸며낸 말이 아니에요—회의에서 사람들이 저한테 소리를 지르곤 했어요. 실제로 야단을 많이 맞았고, 심지어 꽤 무례하게 나가 달라고 하기도 했어요. 저는 "이해가 안 돼요"라고 말했어요.
text_zh: 然后我就去参加这些会议，我没有夸大啊，真的会有人在会上冲我发火。我被人骂。实际上，还有人很不客气地让我离开，我当时就想，"我真搞不明白。"
text_es: Y me iba a estas reuniones, y no me lo estoy inventando, la gente me gritaba en plena junta. Me gritaban. De hecho, me pedían que me fuera, pero nada amables, y yo pensaba, "No entiendo."
original_text: And I would go and have these meetings, and I'm not making this up, people would yell at me in the meeting. I would get yelled at. In fact, I would be asked not very kindly to leave, and I'd be like, "I don't understand. What are you yelling... Why are you mad at me? You asked me for this meeting." And they'd be like... I'm just telling you what I witnessed with my own eyes. We at IMVU, we shipped product 50 times a day on average at a time when people were lucky to be doing it monthly if they were really advanced.

vocabulary.definition: Structured gatherings of individuals to discuss specific topics, make decisions, or share information.
vocabulary.businessContext: In business, meetings are essential for collaboration, project updates, and strategic planning, though they can sometimes be seen as unproductive if not well-managed.
vocabulary.nuance: The effectiveness of meetings can vary greatly; they are often criticized for being too frequent or poorly organized, which can lead to frustration among participants.

text: We charge onto the field and no other army ever came to charge us back, just we won by default because the people who were doing it the old way didn't really like it or want... It was very few defenders of the old way.
speaker: Eric Ries
context: Lenny asks about the current state of the Lean Startup movement. Eric explains how he expected the movement to face fierce opposition from traditional business methodologies, using a military metaphor to describe the anticipated 'battle of ideas.' However, he was surprised to discover there were very few people defending old product development approaches like Stage-Gate methodology - the victory came by default rather than through intellectual combat.
text_ko: 우리가 먼저 시장에 뛰어들었는데, 아무도 우리에게 맞서 싸우러 나오지 않았어요. 결국 예전 방식으로 하던 사람들 자체가 그걸 별로 좋아하지도, 원하지도 않아서 그냥 자동으로 이긴 거예요. 옛 방식을 옹호하는 사람들도 거의 없었어요.
text_zh: 我们冲到战场上，结果发现根本没有其他军队来和我们对抗，就这样不战而胜了，因为那些还在用老方法的人其实自己都不太喜欢那套做法，也不是真心想要...真正为老方法站台的人很少。
text_es: Salimos a la cancha y ningún otro equipo se nos enfrentó, básicamente ganamos sin competencia porque la gente que hacía las cosas a la antigua no les gustaba realmente o no querían... Había muy pocos que defendieran el método tradicional.
key_sentence: We won by default with few defenders of the old way.
original_text: We charge onto the field and no other army ever came to charge us back, just we won by default because the people who were doing it the old way didn't really like it or want... It was very few defenders of the old way. There were very few people who came out and said, "Actually, no, Stage-Gate is actually still the correct product idea. You've got it wrong." It never happened.

vocabulary.definition: Individuals or groups that advocate for or protect a particular idea, practice, or system, often in the face of criticism or change.
vocabulary.businessContext: In a corporate setting, defenders may be employees or stakeholders who resist changes to established practices, often arguing for the value of continuity and stability.
vocabulary.nuance: The term can carry a positive connotation of loyalty but may also imply resistance to necessary change, depending on the context.

vocabulary.definition: To enter a situation or environment with enthusiasm and determination, often implying a proactive approach to challenges.
vocabulary.businessContext: In the business world, this phrase can describe a bold entry into a competitive market or the aggressive pursuit of new opportunities, reflecting a dynamic and assertive strategy.
vocabulary.nuance: This expression evokes imagery of action and decisiveness, making it suitable for contexts that emphasize initiative and courage, but may not be appropriate for more cautious or conservative approaches.

text: I wrote an article, God, five or 10 years ago. God, I can't even remember how many years ago now.
speaker: Eric Ries
context: Lenny asks Eric about misconceptions regarding Lean Startup that frustrate him most. Eric recalls writing an article years ago addressing common misunderstandings about his methodology. The biggest misconception is that 'lean' means 'cheap' and that Lean Startup companies shouldn't raise venture capital. He expresses frustration that despite years of clarification, these same misconceptions persist unchanged in the startup community.
text_ko: 정말, 그 기사 아마 5년? 10년쯤 전에 썼던 것 같아요. 지금은 정확히 몇 년 전인지도 기억이 안 나요.
text_zh: 我写过一篇文章，天哪，五年前还是十年前来着。天哪，我现在都记不清到底是多少年前了。
text_es: Escribí un artículo hace, no sé, cinco o diez años ya. Dios, ya ni me acuerdo hace cuánto fue.
key_sentence: I can't even remember how many years ago now.
original_text: I wrote an article, God, five or 10 years ago. God, I can't even remember how many years ago now. It was like Top Misconceptions About Lean Startup, and it was like, "Number one, lean means cheap, so if you're doing Lean Startup, it means you're not raising money." And it's like, "That's not true." And then kind of I remember what they are... And they're all still prevalent, nothing's changed. I could write that same article today.

text: But the thing that gets missed from the story is that Facebook's already started at that point, it's already being successful, and they're on the break between semesters on the summer.
speaker: Eric Ries
context: Lenny asks about pivoting and how common it is for startups to change direction completely. Eric shares a lesser-known Facebook story to illustrate how even successful founders can miss recognizing their breakthrough products. He describes how Mark Zuckerberg and his co-founders were living in Palo Alto during summer break, working on other projects instead of Facebook, even though Facebook was already showing success - demonstrating how difficult it can be to recognize when you've found product-market fit.
text_ko: 그런데 이야기에서 놓치기 쉬운 건, 그때 이미 페이스북은 시작해서 어느 정도 성공을 거두고 있었고, 그들이 여름 학기 사이의 방학 중이었다는 점이에요.
text_zh: 但是大家忽略的一点是，当时Facebook其实已经起步了，而且已经做得挺成功的，他们正好赶上暑假学期之间的空档。
text_es: Pero lo que se pierde en la historia es que Facebook ya había arrancado en ese momento, ya estaba funcionando bien, y estaban en las vacaciones de verano entre semestres.
key_sentence: the thing that gets missed from the story is that Facebook's already started at that point, it's already being successful
original_text: But the thing that gets missed from the story is that Facebook's already started at that point, it's already being successful, and they're on the break between semesters on the summer. And Dustin Moskovitz, and Mark Zuckerberg, and Adam D'Angelo, and I forget who else are living in this house together. Someone told me this story about what they were actually working on at that time. It wasn't Facebook.

vocabulary.definition: Achieving desired aims or attaining prosperity, often measured by financial performance or market impact.
vocabulary.businessContext: In a business context, being successful typically refers to reaching key performance indicators (KPIs), gaining market share, or achieving profitability.
vocabulary.nuance: The term can carry different meanings depending on the context; for instance, a startup may be considered successful if it meets initial funding goals, even if it is not yet profitable.

text: So first of all, if you're asking whether you should pivot or not you probably know the answer already. That's the first thing to just straight up say.
speaker: Eric Ries
context: Lenny asks Eric for tactical advice on how founders should decide whether to pivot or stay the course, especially relevant for struggling startups. Eric provides a blunt reality check: if founders have time to contemplate whether they should pivot, they probably already know they need to. He explains that true product-market fit creates such overwhelming demand and urgency that founders don't have time for philosophical discussions - they're too busy handling growth.
text_ko: 우선, 피벗(pivot)을 할지 말지를 스스로 묻고 있다면, 아마 이미 답을 알고 있을 거예요. 그걸 제일 먼저 그냥 솔직하게 말해요.
text_zh: 首先啊，如果你在纠结要不要转型(pivot)，其实心里多半已经有答案了。这话我就直说了。
text_es: Bueno, primero que nada, si te estás preguntando si deberías pivotar o no, probablemente ya sabes la respuesta. Eso es lo primero que hay que decir sin rodeos.
key_sentence: if you're asking whether you should pivot or not you probably know the answer already.
original_text: So first of all, if you're asking whether you should pivot or not you probably know the answer already. That's the first thing to just straight up say. People call me sometimes they're like "I want to know if I have product market fit." Well, the fact that you have time to call me and ask me this question already tells me the answer. If you have had product-market fit you would not have time for this.

vocabulary.definition: To pivot means to make a significant change in strategy or direction while maintaining core elements of a business model.
vocabulary.businessContext: In the startup world, pivoting often refers to altering a product or service in response to market feedback or changing circumstances to better meet customer needs.
vocabulary.nuance: The term suggests a strategic and thoughtful change rather than a hasty or reckless decision.

text: The aperture of possible futures that AI makes possible is so incredibly wide. And Predicting it requires a really deep understanding of a bunch of empirical questions, as far as I can tell, nobody knows the answers to right now.
speaker: Eric Ries
context: Lenny asks about how AI is changing the lean startup approach and product development. Eric addresses the uncertainty many people feel about AI's impact on business and society. He explains his framework for taking ethical action despite not knowing what the future holds - the range of possible AI outcomes is so vast that even experts are still researching fundamental questions, so individuals shouldn't feel paralyzed by their lack of expertise.
text_ko: AI가 열어주는 가능한 미래의 지평(aperture of possible futures)이 정말 엄청나게 넓어요. 그리고 그걸 예측하려면, 제 생각엔 지금 아무도 답을 모르는 여러 실증적 질문들(empirical questions)에 대해 정말 깊은 이해가 필요해요.
text_zh: AI带来的未来可能性简直太广了，范围大得不得了。要预测这些变化，你得对很多实际问题有非常深入的理解，但据我观察，现在没人真正知道答案。
text_es: El abanico de futuros posibles que abre la IA es impresionante. Y para predecir qué va a pasar, necesitas entender a fondo un montón de cuestiones empíricas que, por lo que veo, nadie tiene claras ahora mismo.
key_sentence: The aperture of possible futures with AI is incredibly wide and not knowable.
original_text: The aperture of possible futures that AI makes possible is so incredibly wide. And Predicting it requires a really deep understanding of a bunch of empirical questions, as far as I can tell, nobody knows the answers to right now. So given that it's not knowable what's going to happen... You're not an expert enough. As far as I can tell nobody knows. The people who are most expert are actively doing the research to try to find out the thing that will help us predict.

vocabulary.definition: Based on observation or experience rather than theory or pure logic; it refers to knowledge gained through direct or indirect observation.
vocabulary.businessContext: In business and technology, empirical data is crucial for making informed decisions, as it relies on actual performance metrics rather than assumptions.
vocabulary.nuance: While 'empirical' emphasizes evidence-based conclusions, it can imply a limitation in theoretical understanding, so it is best used when discussing data-driven insights.

vocabulary.definition: The ability to grasp the meaning, significance, or nature of something; it involves comprehension and insight into a subject.
vocabulary.businessContext: In a business context, a deep understanding of market dynamics, customer behavior, or technological trends is essential for strategic planning and decision-making.
vocabulary.nuance: The term can suggest a level of expertise or familiarity, so it is often used to convey depth of knowledge rather than superficial awareness.
